nameStory: The name "Wooden Soldiers" comes from this lichen's distinctive upright, slender stalks that stand at attention like tiny military figures marching across rotting wood. Unlike its famous red-capped cousin the British Soldier lichen, these soldiers wear more muted colors but maintain that same proud, vertical posture that makes them look like nature's own toy army.
description: Wooden Soldiers Lichen is a small cup lichen that grows in neat formations of slender, upright stalks rising from a base of tiny scale-like pieces. Each stalk typically reaches about half an inch tall and is topped with a small cup or funnel-shaped structure. The overall color ranges from pale greenish-gray to brownish, and colonies often look like miniature forests of goblets sprouting from decaying wood. This lichen is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Produces distinctive upright, unbranched stalks (called podetia) that rise like tiny soldiers from a base of small, overlapping scales

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing on rotting wood, particularly old logs and decaying stumps with soft, punky texture

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale greenish-gray to brownish when dry, becoming more vibrant green when moist; lacks the bright red caps of British Soldier lichen

idTips.label: Cup Structure
idTips.description: Stalks topped with small, funnel or cup-shaped openings that feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual stalks typically 1/4 to 1/2 inch tall, growing in small colonies that carpet sections of rotting wood

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly granular surface on stalks, with the basal scales feeling papery and overlapping like tiny shingles

habitat: Wooden Soldiers Lichen inhabits decaying wood in moist, shaded forest environments throughout New England's mixed and coniferous woodlands. Look for it on old, soft logs and stumps that have reached an advanced stage of decay, particularly in areas with consistent humidity and protection from direct sunlight. It seems to prefer the secondary xylem (inner wood layers) of decomposing hardwoods and conifers in undisturbed forest settings.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the gray-green colors intensify and the cup structures appear most pronounced. This is an excellent time for photography as the lichen looks fresh and well-hydrated.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat faded during dry periods, with colors shifting to more brownish tones. The stalks remain sturdy but cup edges might curl slightly inward during drought conditions.
seasonality.fall: Often looks refreshed by autumn moisture, displaying good color contrast against fallen leaves. The persistent structures make identification reliable even as surrounding vegetation changes.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable under snow cover, though colors may appear muted. Ice formation in cups can create interesting crystal formations that highlight the structure.

funFact: Wooden Soldiers Lichen is so rare in New England that it has been documented only once in the region, making it one of our most elusive lichen species - finding one would be like discovering a botanical unicorn in your local forest!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small cup lichens like Common Powderhorn or Pixie Cups, but Wooden Soldiers' exclusive preference for rotting wood (rather than soil or moss) is the key difference. Remember: "Wooden Soldiers march on wood" - if you find cup lichens on soil, bark, or rocks, you're looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: The term "cup lichen" refers to the funnel or cup-shaped reproductive structures (apothecia) at the tips of the stalks, which are actually the lichen's way of producing spores. The word "podetia" (singular: podetium) is the technical term for these upright stalks that many Cladonia species produce.
compareHints: Unlike British Soldier lichen which has bright red caps and grows on various surfaces, Wooden Soldiers lacks colorful tops and sticks strictly to decaying wood. It's much less branched than reindeer lichens and more upright than the spreading pixie cups. The wood-only habitat and simple, soldier-like stance distinguish it from the dozens of other Cladonia relatives that prefer soil, moss, or live bark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: British soldier lichen differs from its Cladonia relatives by having consistently red-topped reproductive structures rather than brown or yellow ones.
Star-tipped Reindeer Lichen stands out from its Cladonia cousins by forming the most distinctly cushion-shaped colonies with the densest branching pattern.
Gray reindeer lichen differs from other Cladonia species by its consistently gray color and terrestrial growth habit - most pixie cup lichens are smaller and many grow on rotting wood.
Among all the Cladonia species in New England, fishnet cladonia is unique for its wide, perforated stalks - no other pixie cup or reindeer lichen has this Swiss cheese appearance.
Common Powderhorn differs from its pixie cup relatives by its consistently powdery, granular surface texture - Pebbled Pixie Cup is much bumpier, while Mealy Pixie Cup is smoother.

Giant Cladonia stands apart from its genus relatives primarily through sheer size—while British Soldier lichens top out around 2 inches and most reindeer lichens form low, branching mats, Giant Cladonia towers above them all.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier lichen or the branched, coral-like growth of reindeer lichens, Dragon Horn has a unique two-tier structure with scaly bases and pointed projections.
Green Reindeer Lichen differs from Gray Reindeer Lichen mainly in color (more greenish tints when wet) and slightly more complex branching patterns.
Unlike British Soldier lichen with its bright red caps on straight stalks, Red-fruited Pixie Cup has an actual cup or goblet shape with red fruiting bodies around the rim.

Many-forked cladonia branches more frequently and regularly than most of its Cladonia relatives—while British soldiers have simple stalks topped with red caps, and reindeer lichens have more irregular branching, many-forked cladonia creates dense networks of repeated Y-shaped forks.
Unlike pixie cup lichens that form neat goblet shapes, Thorn Lichen branches end in sharp points.
Dixie Reindeer Lichen is distinguished from other Cladonia species by its consistently small size and extremely fine, dense branching pattern.
Unlike its cousin the British Soldier Lichen which has bright red caps on shorter, more robust stalks, Lipstick Powderhorn has taller, more slender trumpet-shaped stalks.
Among its Cladonia relatives, trumpet lichen's fringed cup edges help distinguish it from the smoother Pebbled Pixie Cup and the bright red-capped British Soldier lichen.
Powder-foot British Soldiers differs from regular British Soldier lichen by its distinctive white powdery base coating on the stalks.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier Lichen or the dense, spongy masses of Reindeer Lichens, Ladder Lichen has a more delicate, architectural appearance.
Among the powderhorn group of Cladonia lichens, Smooth-footed stands out for its clean, uncoated stems and preference for very rotten wood.
Compared to its close relative Gray Reindeer Lichen, Dune Reindeer Lichen is much smaller and more delicate, forming low cushions rather than tall, prominent clumps.
Unlike the smooth, waxy Pebbled Pixie Cup or the bright red-capped British Soldier lichen, Mealy Pixie Cup is distinguished by its powdery, dusty coating and consistently pale coloration.
Unlike the tall, elegant cups of Trumpet Lichen or the branching antler-like forms of reindeer lichens, Stubby-stalked Cladonia keeps a low profile with its characteristic short stalks.
Unlike cup-forming cladonias such as pixie cups or powderhorns, fence-rail cladonia lacks the distinctive cup or funnel shapes at branch tips.
Unlike its smooth-surfaced cousin the Mealy Pixie Cup, this species has that distinctive gritty texture.
Unlike the branched antler-like structures of reindeer lichens or the cup-shaped forms of pixie cup lichens, Smooth Horn Lichen produces simple, unbranched tubes.
Gritty British soldiers differs from regular British soldier lichen by its distinctly rough, gritty stalk texture and lack of powdery soredia.
Unlike the wider cups of Pebbled Pixie Cup or the branched trumpets of Trumpet Lichen, Quill Lichen produces distinctively narrow, unbranched tubes.
Unlike the British Soldier lichens with their bright red caps, or the Pebbled Pixie Cups with their eventual tall stalks, Stalkless Cladonia stays perpetually low and cup-shaped.

Among the many Cladonia species in New England, Olive Cladonia stands out for its distinctive olive-green coloration - most other cup lichens are gray-green (like Mealy Pixie Cup) or have bright red tips (like British Soldier Lichen).
Among its Cladonia relatives, Mealy Forked Cladonia stands out for its powdery coating - most other forked species like Many-forked Cladonia have smooth surfaces.
Unlike British soldier lichen with its bright red caps or the branching patterns of reindeer lichens, wand lichen maintains simple, unbranched points.
Among the reindeer lichens, Black-footed stands out with its dark base coloration - Gray Reindeer Lichen is uniformly pale, while Star-tipped Reindeer Lichen has distinctive star-shaped branch tips.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier Lichen or the branching antler-like form of reindeer lichens, Powdered Funnel Lichen has simple, unbranched cups with a distinctive powdery coating.
Unlike the solid-walled Pebbled Pixie Cup or Mealy Pixie Cup, Sieve Lichen's perforated walls are unmistakable once you know what to look for.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldiers or the branching antler-like growth of Reindeer Lichens, Toy Soldiers maintains the simple cup form throughout its life cycle.
Unlike the neat cup-forming pixie cups or the branching reindeer lichens in its genus, Crazy Scale Lichen stays low and scaly throughout its life.
Unlike the unbranched cups of pebbled pixie cup or the red-capped British soldier lichen, finger cup lichen always shows distinctive branching projections from its cups.
Unlike the familiar gray reindeer lichen which grows in tall, branching cushions, Labrador Prostrate Cladonia stays flat against the ground.
Unlike the common Pebbled Pixie Cup which has simple unbranched cups, Branched Pixie-cup develops complex networks of forked branches from its cups.
Among its Cladonia relatives, Greater Sulphur-cup stands out for its intense yellow coloring - much brighter than the pale yellows of Common Powderhorn or the reds of British Soldier Lichen.
Among the ladder-forming Cladonias, Slender Ladder Lichen is distinguished by its particularly thin stalks and compact size.

Among its Cladonia relatives, Organ-pipe Lichen stands out for its dramatically flared cup openings - while Trumpet Lichen and various powderhorns have tubes, none have the distinctive organ-pipe flare.

Among the many Cladonia species in New England, Browned Pixie-cup stands out for its brownish cup coloration - most of its relatives like Pebbled Pixie Cup or Mealy Pixie Cup have gray or whitish cups.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier Lichen or the obvious cups of Pebbled Pixie Cup, Antlered Powderhorn focuses its energy on intricate branching rather than showy reproductive structures.
Unlike the common Pebbled Pixie Cup which forms simple, single cups, graduated cup lichen creates distinctive tiered structures.
Unlike the bright red caps of British Soldier lichen or the branching antler-like forms of reindeer lichens, turban cup lichen maintains a simple cup-on-stalk structure.
Unlike the more common British Soldier lichen which has distinctly cup-shaped structures before developing red caps, Southern Soldiers tends to branch more directly into its red-topped forms.

Fig-leaved Pixie Lichen stands out from its Cladonia relatives by having proportionally larger, more distinctly leaf-shaped basal scales compared to species like British Soldier Lichen or Common Powderhorn.
Unlike the common British Soldier lichen with its bright red caps, or the branching reindeer lichens, this species maintains the classic small cup shape but in a much more diminutive package.

Among its Cladonia relatives, Rosette Pixie-cup stands out for its neat rosette clustering pattern, unlike the more randomly scattered cups of Pebbled Pixie Cup or the branching, antler-like forms of reindeer lichens.
Reindeer Lichen differs from its close relative Gray Reindeer Lichen by its denser, more cushion-like growth form and tendency to branch in groups of 3-4 rather than mainly in pairs.
